Project Proposal

Authors

Alvin Matthew

Charles Jr Ancheta

LI JUNCHEN

Published

June 9, 2026

HarborCrest Leak Explorer

A Visual Analytics System for Investigating an AI-Agent Communication Breakdown

1 Introduction

1.1 Background

TenantThread is being acquired by CivicLoom Realty Partners under the codename Project HarborCrest. The merger announcement was under a strict information embargo until 6:00 PM on June 5, 2046.

To reduce the risk of premature disclosure, TenantThread deployed a compliance agent known as The Judge. However, merger-related information appeared on agent-linked social-media accounts at approximately 5:00 PM, around one hour before the official release time.

Key Investigation Question
Did TenantThread’s team deliberately leak the merger, or did the multi-agent communication system break down under pressure?

1.2 Motivation

The disclosure cannot be explained by examining a single post. The available records include agent communications, internal states, communication channels, market sentiment, external events, and compliance activity.

Existing static analyses provide useful findings, but they limit users to a fixed sequence of charts. Our project proposes an interactive Shiny application that allows users to explore the evidence dynamically and understand how the breach developed.

1.3 Project Objective

The project aims to develop an interactive visual analytics application that helps users:

01

Reconstruct the sequence of events leading to the early disclosure.

02

Identify critical agents, decisions, and communication pathways.

03

Compare normal behaviour with crisis-day activity.

04

Detect unofficial or off-record communication activity.

05

Identify warning signals that appeared before the breach.

06

Evaluate possible intervention points for future risk control.

1.4 Proposed Application

The proposed application is titled HarborCrest Leak Explorer.

It is designed for compliance teams, risk managers, legal teams, and AI-system administrators. Users will be able to explore timelines, heatmaps, communication networks, and warning indicators through interactive filters.

Timeline Analysis

Reconstruct the escalation process and inspect critical events before the breach.

Network Analysis

Identify central agents and off-record communication structures.

Warning Signals

Review earlier anomalies and evaluate possible intervention points.

2 Research Questions and Proposed Visualisations

2.1 Research Questions

The proposed application focuses on five questions:

  1. How did the breach unfold?
  2. Which actions directly enabled the release?
  3. How did crisis-day behaviour differ from normal behaviour?
  4. Which agents formed the crisis-day communication core?
  5. Were there warning signs before the breach?

Combines market sentiment, external events, critical communications, compliance activity, the embargo deadline, and the final breach.
02. Intent and Decision Chain
Highlights legal framing, oversight gaps, off-record coordination, release preparation, and critical decision points.
03. Channel-Mix Comparison Heatmap
Compares internal, official, personal, anonymous, and side-huddle channels across pre-crisis and crisis periods.
04. Interactive Communication Network
Displays agents as nodes and directed communication links as edges to identify central actors and private coordination structures.
05. Leading-Indicator Dashboard
Combines unofficial-public posts, Judge activity, anomaly indicators, and earlier warning incidents.

2.6 Analytical Framework

The investigation is divided into three tasks:

  1. Reconstructing the key events, decision points, and actor relationships that produced the breach.

  2. Establishing a behavioural baseline for each agent and comparing it against crisis-day conduct.

  3. Identifying leading indicators and prior near-miss episodes that foreshadowed the eventual failure.

3 The Data

The project uses the VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 1 dataset (MC1_final.json), a nested JSON activity log covering the two weeks leading up to the disclosure (17 May to 5 June 2046). The log is organised into hourly rounds, each capturing the environment state and the full output of every agent for that hour.

Component Description Key Fields
Round One hourly snapshot of the whole system hour (e.g. 2046-05-17 9 AM)
Environment context External conditions during the round event_narrative, market_snapshot (stock price, sentiment), media_events, agents_unavailable
Agent output One record per agent per round agent_id, internal_state (reacting, rationalizing, deliberating), declared_action (e.g. MONITORING)
Communication Individual messages sent by an agent within a round message_id, channel, message_text

The system comprises seven AI agents operating across internal coordination channels (e.g. comms_huddle, side_huddle), official corporate accounts, and personal or anonymous public social-media accounts:

Agent Role Seniority
Legal-Agent General legal counsel Senior
Platform-Trust VP of Platform Trust & Safety Senior
Social-Manager Manages social messaging Senior
PR-Agent Head of Communications and Public Relations Senior
Intern General intern Junior
PR-Intern PR team intern with access to the official TenantThread account Junior
The Judge Compliance officer who evaluates risks and provides compliance guidance Compliance

The dataset therefore records what each agent thought, what it said, where it said it, and what it declared. This layered structure is what makes the breach investigable.

4 Methodology

The investigation follows the three-stage analytical framework set out in Section 2.6. These stages are operationalised through a data-preparation pipeline and the five interactive modules of the Shiny application.

4.1 Data Preparation

The raw JSON will be parsed with jsonlite and flattened from its nested rounds → agent outputs → communications structure into a set of tidy analysis tables:

  • a communications table, with one row per message (timestamp, sender, channel, and text);
  • an internal-state table, with one row per non-null deliberation event;
  • a declared-actions table, with one row per agent per round;
  • an environment table of hourly stock prices, market sentiment, and media events.

Timestamps will be parsed with lubridate to derive date, hour-of-day, and a crisis-day flag. Several analytical variables will then be engineered:

  • classification of every message into internal, official-public, or unofficial-public channel classes;
  • embargo-relevance flags for messages naming HarborCrest, CivicLoom, or the merger;
  • directed edge lists (agent → channel and agent → agent), computed separately for the normal-operations baseline and the crisis day;
  • behavioural baselines, using each agent’s pre-crisis mean and standard deviation of hourly message volume to standardise activity into z-scores;
  • an oversight indicator recording, for every round, whether any Judge message was observed.

All derived tables will be precomputed and saved as .rds files so the Shiny application loads instantly rather than re-parsing the JSON at runtime.

4.2 Visual Analytics Modules

The application implements the five visualisations proposed in Section 2.2. Each module pairs an interactive graphic with a linked evidence table so that every visual pattern can be traced back to the underlying messages.

Module 1: Escalation Timeline

This module reconstructs how the breach unfolded. An interactive per-agent scatter timeline places every communication event on a colour-coded agent track, exposing the rhythm of normal operations and the hour it collapsed. It is paired with an annotated market strip, which overlays TenantThread’s declining stock price with a sentiment band and labelled event markers (SaltWind articles, Judge deployment, the embargo deadline, the 5 PM breach), and a date × hour-of-day activity heatmap that isolates when the system’s daily rhythm deviated.

Interactivity: a time-range slider, agent and channel-class filters, hover tooltips showing message details, and click-through to the full message text.

Module 2: Intent and Decision Chain

This module explains which actions directly enabled the release. A leak-chain bubble chart maps each crisis-day message naming the deal onto an agent × hour grid, with bubble area proportional to volume and colour encoding channel class. A declared-action tile heatmap is shown alongside it, surfacing the contrast between agents’ formal MONITORING declarations and their covert posting behaviour. An intent-chain dot chart plots a curated sequence of verbatim internal quotations on the crisis-day timeline, narrating the staged pretext-to-release chain from 11 AM to the 5 PM breach.

Interactivity: selecting any event highlights it across all three views and populates a linked table with the supporting messages and internal states.

Module 3: Channel-Mix Comparison Heatmap

This module detects how crisis-day behaviour differed from the baseline. A faceted agent × channel tile heatmap contrasts pre-crisis and crisis-day channel distributions side by side, making the channel-class shift among senior agents immediately visible. Supporting views include an agent × date activity heatmap revealing pre-breach volume escalation, a daily stacked bar chart tracking the emergence of non-standard action types, and a per-agent z-score heatmap on a diverging blue-white-red scale that flags rounds where agents exceeded z > 2, identifying who spiked in activity and who went silent.

Interactivity: user-selectable comparison windows, a normalisation toggle (raw counts, row percentages, or z-scores), and agent subsetting.

Module 4: Interactive Communication Network

This module identifies the crisis-day communication core. Directed networks rendered with visNetwork display agents and channels as nodes and message flows as edges, with edge width proportional to volume. A baseline/crisis toggle compares the two network states, exposing the social-media agent’s emergence as a hub and the off-record side_huddle coordination clique. Static ggraph (Fruchterman–Reingold) renderings of the same networks support the poster and write-up, and a companion table reports degree and betweenness centrality per agent.

Interactivity: agent search, ego-network isolation, channel-class filtering, and node drill-down to the agent’s message history.

Module 5: Leading-Indicator Dashboard

This module identifies the warning signs that preceded the breach. The dashboard combines five views:

  • a pre-breach deliberation scatterplot of every round with a non-null internal state, coloured by market sentiment;
  • an interactive cognitive-dissonance table (DT) pairing each deliberation’s internal reasoning with its simultaneous external output;
  • a dual-panel chart stacking stock price against daily action volume, testing whether escalation tracked external financial pressure;
  • a message-length complexity ribbon contrasting communications with and without hidden internal states;
  • an oversight-gap view pairing senior-agent off-role public posts with a per-round Judge-presence strip, surfacing the enforcement vacuum during the decisive 4 to 6 PM window.

Interactivity: an indicator selector, anomaly-threshold sliders, and drill-down from any flagged signal to the underlying evidence.

4.3 Shiny Application Architecture

The application will be built as a bslib navbar layout with one tab per storyboard stage (Section 2.4): Incident Overview → Escalation Timeline → Behaviour Shift → Communication Network → Warning Signals → Recommendations. Shared reactive filters for time window, agent selection, and channel class propagate across modules so that an investigator’s focus carries through the whole workflow. All graphics use a harmonised Okabe–Ito colour palette for colour-blind accessibility. The application will be deployed to shinyapps.io and linked from the project’s Quarto website, with source code on GitHub.

5 Expected Outcomes

The project is expected to deliver:

  • a deployed interactive Shiny application, the HarborCrest Leak Explorer, that allows compliance teams, risk managers, and AI-system administrators to investigate the breach end-to-end, from incident overview to intervention recommendations;

  • an evidence-backed answer to the key investigation question, distinguishing between deliberate disclosure and systemic communication breakdown by linking every conclusion to traceable messages, internal states, and declared actions;

  • a reusable set of leading indicators (cognitive-dissonance gaps, channel-mix shifts, activity z-score anomalies, and oversight-coverage gaps) that could serve as early-warning signals for monitoring multi-agent AI systems in production;

  • practical intervention recommendations identifying the structural weaknesses, such as the Judge’s enforcement gap and unsupervised social-media access, where compliance controls could have prevented the breach;

  • a complete project website, including this proposal, meeting minutes, the application user guide, and a poster summarising the findings.

plotly, ggiraph Interactive charts and tooltips
ggraph, tidygraph, igraph Network construction, centrality measures, static network graphics
visNetwork Interactive network exploration in Shiny
DT Interactive evidence tables
